title: Indirect Tax Is Charged on Transactions, Not on Profit
summary: Value added tax, goods and services tax and customs duties are charged when things are bought, sold or imported, whether or not the project ever makes money. This lesson teaches how the credit mechanism works, why exempt residential rent turns tax into cost, and what an investment concession really is.
body:
Income tax waits for profit; indirect tax arrives with every invoice and every container, so a developer who ignores it until the end discovers it as a cost that was baked into the building years earlier.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 61?

A. Never set an intercompany price without a written analysis, made at the time, of the whole bundle the payment buys, tested against comparables that buy the same bundle.

Q. In thin capitalisation, what is an earnings test?

A. A rule capping net interest deductions at a percentage of a measure of earnings. It can allow little or nothing during construction, when earnings are zero.

Q. In owner's project management, what is an owner decision log?

A. A dated record of every decision the owner makes, who made it, on what information, and what it changed, so later disputes are argued from the record rather than from memory.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, indirect taxes do not appear on a profit and loss statement in the way income tax does, so developers forget them. Yet on a construction project they touch almost every payment: the contractor's invoices, the consultants' fees, imported equipment, the sale of finished units and, in some places, rent. Whether that tax is recovered or becomes part of your cost can move a project's budget by a meaningful percentage. And in many developing economies, relief from these taxes is the core of what an investment concession offers, so understanding them is understanding the deal you negotiate with government.

How value added tax works

Plain English. Value added tax (VAT), called goods and services tax (GST) in some countries, is charged by a registered business on what it sells and paid by the buyer. The business then deducts the tax it paid on its own purchases and pays the government only the difference. Each business in the chain pays tax on the value it added, and the final consumer, who cannot deduct anything, bears the whole tax.

The professional framing is two ledgers. Output tax is the tax you charge on your sales. Input tax is the tax you pay on your purchases. If your sales are taxable, you can usually claim the input tax back as an input tax credit. If output exceeds input, you pay the difference; if input exceeds output, as it often does during construction, you may be owed a refund. Verify every rate, threshold and refund rule against the primary source before you rely on it.

Taxable, zero-rated and exempt

Every sale falls into one of three categories, and the category decides whether you recover your input tax. A taxable supply carries tax at a positive rate and gives full credit for related input tax. A zero-rated supply carries tax at zero percent and still gives full credit, which is how many countries treat exports. An exempt supply carries no tax, and the seller gets no credit for the input tax on purchases used to make it.

That last point is the trap. Exempt sounds favourable. It is not, for the supplier. In many countries the long-term rental of residential property is exempt. A developer building an apartment block to rent therefore pays VAT on construction and cannot recover it. That tax becomes part of the cost of the building. A developer building the same block to sell new units may find the first sale of new residential property taxable, and recover the input tax. The category depends on the law of each country; verify against the primary source.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example one: rent or sell

A hypothetical project costs 20,000,000 dollars before VAT, all of it on taxable purchases. Assume a hypothetical VAT rate of 10 percent, taken from no country. Input tax is 2,000,000 dollars.

Case A: the developer sells new units, and in this hypothetical the sale is taxable. The 2,000,000 dollars is recoverable, either as a refund during construction or as a credit against output tax on the sales. The cost of the building is 20,000,000 dollars. The cash cost is the funding of 2,000,000 dollars until it is recovered.

Case B: the developer keeps the building and rents the apartments, and in this hypothetical residential rent is exempt. The 2,000,000 dollars is not recoverable. The cost of the building is 22,000,000 dollars. On net operating income of 1,400,000 dollars, yield on cost falls from 7.0 percent to about 6.4 percent, purely from indirect tax.

A mixed-use building, with shops on the ground floor and apartments above, sits between the two, and input tax must be apportioned. Day 3 prices that.

Customs duties and the investment concession

Customs duty is a tax on goods as they cross a border into a country, calculated on the customs value of the goods according to their tariff classification, a code from an internationally used system that groups goods by type. Import VAT is often charged at the border as well. Unlike VAT, customs duty is usually not recoverable as a credit; it is a cost.

Worked example two. A developer imports elevators, generators and cladding with a hypothetical customs value of 3,000,000 dollars. At a hypothetical duty rate of 10 percent, duty is 300,000 dollars, a direct cost. If the developer holds an investment concession that waives duty on approved items for an approved project, that 300,000 dollars is saved, but only on the items listed, only for that project, and only if the conditions are met.

An investment concession is an agreement or approval by which a government grants relief from taxes or duties, for example customs duty waivers, VAT relief on imports or a period of reduced income tax, in exchange for commitments such as a minimum investment, jobs, completion by a date or use of the goods only in the approved project. It is a contract with conditions, not a gift.

How the best do it

Experienced developers treat indirect tax as a design input from the first pro forma. They run the budget both gross and net of recoverable tax, decide early whether each part of the building is for sale or for rent, structure the entity so the right company is registered, and keep a concession register that ties every relieved import to its approved use. A small developer can copy this with one extra column in the budget, "recoverable or not", and one spreadsheet listing every concession condition with its deadline.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the category of each supply decides recovery; verify each country's rules against the primary source. Liability: concession conditions are legal obligations, and breach can mean repayment with interest and penalties. Banking: lenders fund VAT during construction and want to see when refunds arrive. Governance: someone named is responsible for VAT returns and concession compliance. Estate: a concession may not transfer automatically to heirs or a new owner. Exit: selling a building can itself be a taxable supply, and changing it from sale to rent can trigger tax.

Professional sign-off required: indirect tax adviser in the project's country; a licensed customs broker for imports.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming all VAT on a project is recoverable. Where any part is exempt, it is not, and the cost hides in the budget. The control is to classify every intended supply at feasibility, with advice, and to carry unrecoverable tax as a cost line.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears "residential rent is exempt" and thinks it is good news. For the landlord who built the building, it usually means the construction VAT is never recovered.

Callback

In Week 23, Devika and Elias drew the real estate tax map: transfer taxes, VAT and GST, gains and recapture. This week goes deeper into one region of that map, and shows that the category of a supply, decided by what you intend to do with the building, is as important as the rate.

Recap

VAT and GST are charged on transactions, with credits for tax paid on purchases used to make taxable or zero-rated supplies, and no credits for exempt ones. Customs duty is usually a pure cost. An investment concession relieves these taxes only within its conditions.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: a composite case of an investment concession clawed back.
checklist: I have classified every intended supply as taxable, zero-rated or exempt, with advice.
My budget shows each cost gross of VAT and states whether the VAT is recoverable.
Unrecoverable VAT is carried as a cost line, not ignored.
I know when VAT refunds arrive and how construction VAT is funded meanwhile.
I know the tariff classification and duty on every major import.
I know every condition and deadline of any investment concession.
A named person is responsible for VAT returns and concession compliance.
An indirect tax adviser and a licensed customs broker have reviewed the plan.
head: Field checklist
speak: Indirect tax is charged on transactions, not profit. Value added tax, or GST, is charged by a registered business on its sales, and it can usually deduct the tax it paid on purchases used to make taxable or zero-rated sales. But for exempt sales, it gets no credit. In many countries long-term residential rent is exempt, so a developer who builds to rent pays construction VAT and never recovers it. In my hypothetical, two million dollars of VAT on a twenty million dollar build became cost, cutting yield on cost from seven percent to about 6.4. Customs duty on imports is usually a pure cost too. An investment concession can waive duty or VAT, but only on approved items, for the approved project, if the conditions are met. So I classify every supply at feasibility, carry unrecoverable tax as cost, and keep a register of every concession condition.
terms: Input tax credit — a deduction of the VAT or GST paid on purchases, available when they are used to make taxable or zero-rated supplies.
Exempt supply — a sale on which no VAT is charged and for which the seller cannot recover the input tax on related purchases.
Investment concession — a government grant of relief from taxes or duties in exchange for defined commitments by the investor.

hostile.q: Your budget shows construction cost net of VAT. You plan to rent the apartments. Who pays the VAT you cannot recover?
hostile.a: The project does, and our revised budget shows it. Our adviser classified the residential leases as exempt, so the VAT on the residential share of construction is a cost of the building, carried as its own line and funded in the sources and uses. The commercial ground floor is taxable, and we apportion input tax between the two on the method the adviser set out. The yield on cost you see already reflects the unrecoverable tax.

title: The Concession That Came Back With Interest
summary: This is a composite example. A developer won a duty and VAT concession for a hotel project, imported materials and equipment under it, moved some to another site, missed a completion condition, and could not prove where the rest went. The relief was clawed back with interest and penalties. Seven steps, ending in Rule 62.
body:
This is a composite example. A concession saved real money at the border, and three years later the same money came back as a demand, larger, because nobody had treated the concession as a contract with conditions.

Recall

Q. What is an exempt supply, and why is it a trap for a landlord who built the building?

A. A sale on which no VAT is charged and for which the seller cannot recover input tax on related purchases. A landlord letting exempt residential space therefore cannot recover the construction VAT.

Q. In the GlaxoSmithKline case, what did the Supreme Court of Canada say the price had to be judged against?

A. All the circumstances an arm's-length purchaser would consider, including the separate licence agreement, not the ingredient price alone.

Q. What is a hold point in a quality plan?

A. A stage in the work beyond which the contractor may not proceed until a named inspector has checked and released it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because a concession is a legal instrument and its breach is a compliance failure, not a bad market. In many emerging markets the concession is a major part of the project's economics. Treat it as income you have not yet earned, because until every condition is met, that is what it is. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

1. Timeline

Year 1: a developer obtains an investment concession for a hotel. It waives customs duty and import VAT on listed construction materials and equipment, on conditions: the goods are used only in the approved hotel, the hotel opens within three years, and records of each import and its use are kept for inspection. Year 1 to year 2: the developer imports goods with a customs value of 5,000,000 dollars, saving hypothetical duty of 500,000 dollars and import VAT of 750,000 dollars. Year 2: to keep a second, smaller project moving, the site manager transfers a container of tiles and two generators to it. Year 3: financing delays push the opening date back by eight months. Year 4: the authority inspects, finds goods it cannot trace, notes the missed opening date, and demands the relieved duty and VAT on all goods, with interest and a penalty.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Moving relieved goods to a project the concession did not cover. Letting the opening date slip without applying for an extension before it passed. And running the import records from the freight forwarder's paperwork rather than from a register the developer controlled.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed the goods were his once they cleared customs. Legally, under many concession regimes, relieved goods remain subject to conditions until the conditions are met. He assumed a short delay to the opening date would be tolerated. And he assumed the authority would argue only about the goods that were moved, not about everything he could not account for.

4. Incentives

The site manager was measured on keeping both projects moving, not on concession compliance. The freight forwarder was paid per shipment, not to track goods after delivery. The developer's attention was on financing. Nobody's job description included the concession.

5. Warning signs ignored

The concession agreement contained a schedule of conditions that nobody had copied into a calendar. The goods arrived in mixed containers with no site-level record of where each item was installed. The opening date was visibly at risk eighteen months before it passed. And when goods were moved, there was no document at all, which means there was no moment at which anyone asked whether it was allowed.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the opening date passing without a written extension. Many concession regimes give the authority wide discretion once a condition is breached. Before the date, an application for an extension, with reasons, would have been an ordinary administrative request. After it, the developer was a party in breach asking for forgiveness, and the untraced goods made the request weaker.

7. Root cause

The root cause was treating the concession as a discount at the border rather than as a contract running for years. Relief was taken at import, but the obligations attached to it, use, timing and records, were managed by nobody. When the authority tested those obligations, the developer could not show he had met them.

Say that out loud now.

What it cost

The relieved amounts were 1,250,000 dollars. In this composite, the authority demanded all of it, because the developer could not prove which relieved goods were installed in the hotel. With interest and a penalty, the demand was materially larger. Had he kept a register, the demand might have been limited to the goods moved to the second site, a fraction of the total, and perhaps settled by paying duty on those goods voluntarily before the inspection.

Cole's view: disclose before you are found

Cole adds a point about the moment the generators left the hotel site. At that moment the developer knew something the authority did not. Many tax and customs systems treat a breach the taxpayer reports and corrects before an inspection very differently from one the authority discovers, sometimes with reduced penalties under a voluntary disclosure process, though whether such a process exists and what it offers must be verified against the primary source. Even where no formal process exists, a taxpayer who comes forward with the facts, the calculation and the payment is in a stronger position in every later conversation.

The decision is rarely made, because nobody escalates the small breach. So the rule inside the company must be that any movement, sale or loss of relieved goods is reported to the concession owner the same week, and that the owner decides with the lawyer whether to disclose. The cost of disclosing two generators is the duty and VAT on two generators. The cost of being found is the loss of credibility that turns every other item into a question.

What a good outcome looked like

A concession register: every imported item, its customs entry, its value and relief, the drawing reference where it is installed, and a photograph once installed. A condition calendar: each obligation, its date, the person responsible and the date to apply for an extension. A rule that no relieved goods leave the approved site without written approval from the concession owner and, where required, the authority. And a quarterly self-audit comparing the register with the site.

Rule 62

Rule 62: Never use a tax or duty concession without a register that ties every relieved item to its approved use, and a dated calendar of every condition, owned by a named person and reviewed every month.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the concession agreement and any extension request; licensed customs broker, on the import records.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the concession is negotiated by the developer and then forgotten by the site. The control is a named owner of the concession, with the register and calendar, reporting monthly to the developer.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts the concession as savings on day one. It is savings only on the day the last condition is met.

Callback

In Week 49, Marco and Quincy taught change control: nothing changes scope without a written change order. Moving relieved goods to another site is a change to the concession's scope made without a change order. The same discipline, written approval before the change, would have stopped it.

Recap

A developer took duty and VAT relief at import, moved some goods to an uncovered project, missed the opening date and kept no register. The authority clawed back everything with interest and a penalty. Rule 62 demands a register, a condition calendar and a named owner.

Next: Sage on The Money: what recoverable and unrecoverable VAT, apportionment and refund timing do to cost and return.
checklist: Every concession has a named owner inside my company.
I keep a register tying each relieved import to its installed location.
I have a dated calendar of every concession condition.
I apply for any extension before the deadline, not after.
No relieved goods leave the approved site without written approval.
I run a quarterly self-audit of the register against the site.
My lawyer has reviewed what happens on breach of each condition.
My customs broker's records reconcile with my register.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. A developer won a concession waiving customs duty and import VAT on materials for a hotel, on conditions: use only in that hotel, open within three years, and keep records. He imported five million dollars of goods and saved 1.25 million. His site manager moved some tiles and generators to another project. Financing delays pushed the opening past the deadline, and nobody applied for an extension. When the authority inspected, he could not show where much of the relieved goods had gone, so it clawed back the whole relief with interest and a penalty. The root cause was treating the concession as a discount at the border rather than a contract running for years. Rule 62: never use a concession without a register that ties every relieved item to its approved use, and a dated calendar of every condition, owned by a named person and reviewed monthly.
terms: Clawback — a demand that relief already given be repaid, usually with interest and sometimes penalties, after a condition is breached.
Concession register — a record tying each relieved item to its customs entry, value, relief and installed location.
Condition calendar — a dated list of every obligation attached to a concession, its owner and its extension deadline.

hostile.q: Your concession required the hotel to open by the end of year three. It did not. Why shouldn't we recover all the relief?
hostile.a: Because we applied for an extension four months before the date, with the reasons and a revised programme, and you acknowledged the application in writing. Every relieved item is in our register with its customs entry and installed location, and the register has been reconciled to the site each quarter. Two generators were moved in error; we identified them ourselves and are ready to pay the duty and VAT on those items now.

rule: Rule 62: Never use a tax or duty concession without a register that ties every relieved item to its approved use, and a dated calendar of every condition, owned by a named person and reviewed every month.

title: VAT in the Cash Flow: Apportionment, Refund Timing and the Cost of Funding It
summary: Even recoverable VAT costs money, because it is paid out before it comes back, and unrecoverable VAT is simply cost. This lesson prices a mixed-use building's apportionment, the funding of construction VAT until refunds arrive, and what both do to yield on cost and return.
body:
Recoverable VAT is a loan you make to the government until the refund arrives, unrecoverable VAT is a permanent cost, and a mixed-use building has both, in a proportion you must decide before the first invoice.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 62?

A. Never use a tax or duty concession without a register that ties every relieved item to its approved use, and a dated calendar of every condition, owned by a named person and reviewed every month.

Q. In a guarantee fee analysis, what is removed before pricing the fee?

A. The benefit of passive association: the better terms a subsidiary gets simply from belonging to the group.

Q. What is the in-balance test in construction lending?

A. The requirement that undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity covers the full cost to complete before any further draw.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, construction lenders fund the budget, and the budget includes VAT. If you have treated VAT as recoverable when part of it is not, the project is short of money from the first day, and the in-balance test will find the gap eventually. If you have treated recoverable VAT as cost-free, you have not funded the months between paying it and getting it back. Both mistakes show up as cash, not as tax. Every rate and figure here is hypothetical, taken from no country; verify each real rule against the primary source.

Apportionment in a mixed-use building

Plain English. A building with shops on the ground floor and rented apartments above makes two kinds of supply: taxable commercial rent and, in this hypothetical, exempt residential rent. Input tax on costs that belong only to the shops is recoverable. Input tax on costs that belong only to the apartments is not. Input tax on shared costs, the structure, the roof, the lifts, must be split between the two by an apportionment method.

The professional framing: countries specify or accept methods such as floor area, expected rent or construction cost; some require the method to be agreed with the authority, and many require a later adjustment if actual use differs from intended use over a period of years. Verify which methods are accepted and whether an adjustment period applies.

Worked example one: the apportionment

Hypothetical facts: a 30,000,000 dollar project before VAT, with a hypothetical 10 percent VAT rate. Costs specific to the shops: 2,000,000 dollars. Costs specific to the apartments: 8,000,000 dollars. Shared costs: 20,000,000 dollars. The shops are 20 percent of floor area, the apartments 80 percent, and floor area is the accepted method.

Step 1, direct shop costs: VAT of 200,000 dollars, fully recoverable. Step 2, direct apartment costs: VAT of 800,000 dollars, not recoverable. Step 3, shared costs: VAT of 2,000,000 dollars, of which 20 percent, 400,000 dollars, is recoverable and 80 percent, 1,600,000 dollars, is not.

Total VAT paid: 3,000,000 dollars. Recoverable: 200,000 plus 400,000, which is 600,000 dollars. Unrecoverable: 800,000 plus 1,600,000, which is 2,400,000 dollars. The true cost of the building is 32,400,000 dollars, not 30,000,000 dollars.

If stabilised net operating income is 2,100,000 dollars, yield on cost is 7.0 percent on the net figure and about 6.48 percent on the true figure. That half point is the indirect tax decision, and it belongs in the first pro forma.

Now suppose expected rent were the accepted method and the shops earn 35 percent of total rent. The recoverable share of shared-cost VAT rises to 700,000 dollars, total recoverable to 900,000 dollars, and cost falls by 300,000 dollars. Method matters, and it must be the one the law and the authority accept, not the one that suits you.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: funding recoverable VAT

Even the 600,000 dollars you will recover must be paid first. Suppose the recoverable VAT is paid evenly over 24 months of construction, about 25,000 dollars a month, and the authority refunds it with a lag of four months, as a hypothetical. At any time about four months of payments, 100,000 dollars, are outstanding, and the balance rises if refunds stall.

At a hypothetical 8 percent construction interest rate, carrying 100,000 dollars for 24 months costs about 100,000 times 0.08 times 2, which is 16,000 dollars. Small here. But if refunds are only available once the building starts making taxable supplies, the whole 600,000 dollars builds up over construction and is funded until after completion. The average balance is then about 300,000 dollars over 24 months, costing about 48,000 dollars, plus the months until the refund arrives. Some lenders offer a separate VAT facility for exactly this, sized to the expected refunds and repaid from them; its terms are commercial practice, not a standard.

Worked example three: the change of plan

Suppose a developer builds apartments for sale, claims all input VAT because new residential sales are taxable in this hypothetical, then cannot sell in a weak market and rents them instead. Many systems then require repayment of some or all of the input tax claimed, because the building is now used for exempt supplies; some spread this over an adjustment period. In this hypothetical, the developer who claimed 2,400,000 dollars on the residential part may have to repay a large share of it in the year the plan changes. That cash call arrives exactly when the project is weakest. Verify against the primary source.

The five questions a lender asks about VAT

When I review a borrower's budget as Priya the lender, I ask five things about indirect tax, and you should have the answers on one page. First, is the budget gross or net of VAT, and which lines carry unrecoverable VAT? Second, which supplies will the project make, taxable, zero-rated or exempt, and who advised on that? Third, what apportionment method is used, and is it accepted under local law? Fourth, when do refunds arrive, and how is the gap funded, by equity, by the construction loan or by a VAT facility? Fifth, what happens if the plan changes, for example from sale to rent, and how large could the repayment of credits be? A borrower who answers those five in a minute tells me the budget was built by someone who understands where the cash goes. A borrower who cannot tells me to send my own adviser, at the borrower's cost.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's view for your personal balance sheet: a VAT refund receivable in a project company is a real asset only when it is approved and its timing is known. Until then, record it at a discount for delay and risk, and never count it as liquidity. And an investment property whose VAT treatment depends on continuing to rent it is less flexible than one that does not; that loss of flexibility is a cost of the asset, even though it appears on no statement. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a budget built net of all VAT on a building that will make exempt supplies. The control is a budget built gross, with an apportionment schedule agreed by your adviser, and a sources-and-uses line for unrecoverable VAT.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats recoverable VAT as free money. It is money paid out early and returned late, and the gap must be funded.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya and Roman taught the in-balance test and the interest reserve. Unrecoverable VAT left out of the budget is an out-of-balance notice waiting to happen, and a stalled VAT refund behaves exactly like a delay: it consumes reserve and equity before anyone has made a mistake on site.

Recap

In a mixed-use building, apportion shared-cost VAT by an accepted method; in this hypothetical 2,400,000 dollars of VAT became cost. Fund recoverable VAT until refunds arrive, and price the risk of a change from sale to rent clawing back credits.

Next: Devika on The Rules: registration, place of supply, customs valuation and classification, and the anatomy of a concession.
checklist: My budget is built gross of VAT, with recoverable and unrecoverable shares shown.
I have an apportionment method for shared costs accepted under local law.
I know whether actual use later triggers an adjustment of credits claimed.
I have modelled the funding of recoverable VAT until refunds arrive.
I know when refunds become available, during construction or only after.
I have priced the cash call if the plan changes from sale to rent.
My sources and uses carry a line for unrecoverable VAT.
I treat a VAT refund receivable as uncertain until approved.
head: Field checklist
speak: VAT hits a project's cash, not just its tax return. In a mixed-use building with taxable shops and exempt rented apartments, input tax on shop costs is recoverable, on apartment costs it is not, and on shared costs it is split by an accepted method, such as floor area. In my hypothetical thirty million dollar building, 2.4 million dollars of VAT became permanent cost, cutting yield on cost by about half a point. The recoverable part still has to be paid before it comes back, so I fund it, perhaps with a VAT facility repaid from refunds. And if I claim credits to build units for sale, then rent them instead, many systems claw back those credits, and the cash call lands when the project is weakest. So I budget gross, apportion by an accepted method, and treat any refund as uncertain until approved.
terms: Apportionment — splitting input tax on shared costs between taxable and exempt uses by an accepted method, such as floor area.
Adjustment period — a period after construction during which a change in actual use can require credits already claimed to be repaid or increased.
VAT facility — a short-term loan sized to expected VAT refunds and repaid from them; its terms are commercial practice.

hostile.q: Your budget assumes all the VAT is recoverable, but the apartments will be rented. Where is the missing 2,400,000 dollars?
hostile.a: You are right that the earlier draft understated cost. The revised budget is built gross: 600,000 dollars of VAT recoverable on the commercial share and the apportioned shared costs, and 2,400,000 dollars unrecoverable on the residential share, carried as its own line and funded in the sources and uses. The apportionment uses floor area, which our adviser confirmed is an accepted method, and the recoverable VAT is funded by a separate facility repaid from refunds.

title: Registration, Place of Supply, Customs Value and the Anatomy of a Concession
summary: Indirect tax rules turn on a small set of questions: who must register, where a supply is made, when tax falls due, how imports are valued and classified, and what a concession actually binds you to. This lesson teaches them as concepts, with two worked examples.
body:
Most indirect tax mistakes on a development are not about the rate; they are about the wrong company being registered, a foreign service nobody taxed, an import valued on the wrong basis, or a concession condition nobody read.

Recall

Q. In a mixed-use building, how is VAT on shared costs treated?

A. It is apportioned between taxable and exempt uses by a method accepted under local law, such as floor area, and only the taxable share is recoverable.

Q. What does a mutual agreement procedure do?

A. It lets the tax authorities of two treaty countries negotiate to eliminate double taxation, including after a transfer pricing adjustment.

Q. Under a design-build delivery method, who carries design risk?

A. Mostly the design-builder, which contracts for both design and construction, though the owner keeps responsibility for its own brief and any design it supplies.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, I teach these as concepts. Every country writes them differently and changes them often. Nothing here states any country's rate, threshold or deadline; verify each point against the primary source before you rely on it. What you need is the list of questions, so you can make your adviser answer each one in writing before the first invoice.

Registration

Plain English. A business must usually register for VAT or GST once its taxable sales exceed a threshold, and may be allowed to register voluntarily below it. Only a registered business can charge VAT and recover input tax.

The professional point for a developer is timing. A project company may make no sales for two or three years while it pays VAT on every construction invoice. If it is not registered, or if the rules allow registration only once sales begin, it may lose input tax or have to wait. Many systems allow a business that intends to make taxable supplies to register early, sometimes with conditions. Ask: which company in my structure makes the supply, must that company register, can it register before it sells anything, and what evidence of intention does the authority want?

A related trap: the parent signs the construction contract and receives the invoices, while the project company owns the land and will make the sales. Input tax is usually recoverable only by the person who received the supply and makes the taxable sales, so in that arrangement it may be recoverable by neither. Contract in the name of the company that will make the supply.

Time and place of supply

Time of supply decides when tax falls due: often the earlier of invoice, payment or delivery. Progress billing on a construction contract can make each payment application a separate supply. A deposit on a pre-sold unit may be taxable when received, not when the unit is delivered. Verify against the primary source.

Place of supply decides which country's VAT applies. Goods are usually taxed where they are delivered or imported. Services are harder. Many systems tax services received by a business where the recipient is, and require the recipient to account for the tax itself on services bought from abroad, a mechanism called the reverse charge.

Worked example one. A project company buys design services from a foreign architect for a hypothetical 500,000 dollars. The architect charges no local VAT. Under a hypothetical reverse charge at 10 percent, the project company must account for 50,000 dollars of output tax on its own return. If its supplies are fully taxable, it claims the same 50,000 dollars back as input tax, so the net cost is zero but the entries must be made. If its supplies are exempt, residential rent for example, the 50,000 dollars is a real cost that nobody invoiced. Developers who miss the reverse charge often discover it at an audit, with interest, on years of foreign consultants' fees.

Say that out loud now.

Change of use and self-supply

If a building is used for something other than what the credits were claimed for, many systems require an adjustment. Some also treat a developer who builds and then rents new residential property as making a deemed sale to itself, a self-supply, on which VAT is charged at the time of first occupation, so the state collects the tax the developer never paid on the exempt rent. Whether a self-supply rule exists, and how value is measured, must be verified.

Customs valuation, classification and origin

Customs duty depends on three things. Value: many countries follow internationally agreed valuation rules based on the transaction value, the price actually paid, adjusted by additions such as freight and insurance to the border where the country's rules require them, and certain royalties or assists. Classification: the tariff code under the internationally used Harmonized System, which decides the duty rate. Origin: where the goods were made, which decides whether a preferential rate under a trade agreement applies.

Worked example two. An elevator package is bought for 400,000 dollars at the factory. Freight to the port of import costs 30,000 dollars and insurance 5,000 dollars. In a hypothetical country that values on cost, insurance and freight, the customs value is 435,000 dollars. At a hypothetical duty rate of 5 percent, duty is 21,750 dollars. Import VAT in many systems is charged on value plus duty: at a hypothetical 10 percent, on 456,750 dollars, that is 45,675 dollars. If the elevators are classified under a different heading, say as general machinery rather than lifts, the duty rate may differ, and an authority that disagrees with your classification will reassess. Ask your customs broker for a written classification, and in significant cases consider applying for a binding ruling where one is available.

The anatomy of a concession

An investment concession is read like a contract. Ask seven questions. What is its legal basis: a statute, a regulation, a ministerial approval or a negotiated agreement? What is relieved: which taxes, on which items, up to what value? Who holds it: the project company, the parent or the contractor? What are the conditions: investment amount, jobs, dates, use of goods, reporting? How is compliance monitored: inspections, returns, certificates? What happens on breach: clawback, interest, penalties, loss of future relief? And can it be transferred: to a lender on enforcement, to a buyer, to an heir? Each answer goes into the concession register and calendar from Rule 62.

Two points developers miss. First, relief granted to the developer may not extend to goods imported by its contractor, so the contract must say who imports, in whose name and who carries the duty if the concession does not apply. Second, a concession often binds the project to a use, a hotel, a factory, for years after completion, which can limit exit options. A buyer will ask whether the concession survives a sale and what happens to past relief if it does not.

Professional sign-off required: indirect tax adviser in the project's country; licensed customs broker; lawyer on the concession instrument.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that indirect tax is handled by the bookkeeper invoice by invoice, with nobody asking the structural questions: which company registers, what is the place of supply of each service, how imports are classified. The control is a one-page indirect tax memo for each project, written at feasibility and updated at each stage gate.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes a foreign consultant's invoice with no VAT on it means no VAT is due. Under a reverse charge, the buyer owes it.

Callback

In Week 52, Marco taught procurement and delivery methods. The import clause in each contract is an indirect tax decision: if the contractor imports in its own name, the developer's concession may not reach the goods. Procurement and indirect tax have to be designed together.

Recap

Ask who registers and when, the time and place of each supply, whether a reverse charge applies to foreign services, whether a change of use or self-supply rule applies, how imports are valued and classified, and seven questions about any concession. Write the answers down before the first invoice.

Next: Devika on The Numbers: reverse engineering a landed cost and an indirect tax overrun.
checklist: I know which company in my structure makes each supply and must register.
I know whether the project company can register before it makes any sales.
I know when tax falls due on progress billings and deposits.
I account for the reverse charge on services bought from abroad.
I know whether a change of use or self-supply rule applies to a build-to-rent project.
Each major import has a written tariff classification and a valuation basis.
I have answered the seven concession questions in writing.
My construction contracts say who imports, in whose name, and who bears duty.
head: Field checklist
speak: Most indirect tax mistakes are not about the rate. They are about the wrong company registered, or a company not registered while it pays years of construction VAT. They are about a foreign architect's invoice with no VAT on it, when a reverse charge means the buyer owes the tax and, if its supplies are exempt, pays it as a real cost. They are about change of use, where renting units that were built for sale claws back credits. And they are about imports: customs value, often price plus freight and insurance, classification under the Harmonized System, and origin. In my hypothetical an elevator package carried both duty and import VAT on top of the price. A concession must be read like a contract: legal basis, what is relieved, who holds it, conditions, monitoring, breach and transfer. I answer all of it in writing before the first invoice.
terms: Reverse charge — a rule requiring the buyer of certain services from abroad to account for the VAT itself instead of the foreign supplier.
Customs value — the value on which duty is calculated, often the price paid plus defined additions such as freight and insurance to the border.
Tariff classification — the code under the Harmonized System that identifies goods for customs purposes and determines the duty rate.

hostile.q: Your project company paid foreign design consultants for three years and never accounted for VAT on those services. Why not?
hostile.a: It should have, and we have identified the gap ourselves. Our adviser has calculated the reverse-charge VAT on every foreign invoice for the three years, the input tax we are entitled to recover on the taxable share, and the net amount due with interest. We would like to correct it now, by voluntary disclosure if that route is available, and we have put a reverse-charge check into our invoice approval process going forward.

title: Reverse Engineering a Landed Cost and an Indirect Tax Overrun
summary: Two calculations worked backward from a finished outcome: from the total paid at the border back to the customs value, duty and import VAT, and from a project that finished over budget back to the indirect tax decisions that caused the overrun. Hypothetical round numbers throughout.
body:
When indirect tax goes wrong, it shows up as a single surprising number, a border payment or a budget overrun, and the skill is to take that number apart, layer by layer, until each piece points to the decision that caused it.

Recall

Q. What is the reverse charge?

A. A rule requiring the buyer of certain services from abroad to account for the VAT itself, instead of the foreign supplier charging it.

Q. In transfer pricing, what is a secondary adjustment?

A. An extra adjustment treating the excess of a non-arm's-length price as a dividend, loan or other payment, which may attract withholding.

Q. In the Last Planner approach, what is a look-ahead?

A. A short-range plan, often several weeks, that identifies the constraints to remove so that planned work is ready to be done when its time comes.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on an even week we reverse engineer. You will often meet indirect tax as a finished fact: a customs broker's invoice, a final cost report. If you can rebuild the number, you can check it, challenge it and find the decision to change next time. Every rate here is hypothetical, taken from no country: customs duty 5 percent, VAT and import VAT 10 percent, import VAT charged on customs value plus duty. Verify every real rule against the primary source.

Calculation one: from the border payment back to the customs value

The outcome: the customs broker reports that 57,750 dollars of duty and import VAT was paid at the border on a shipment of generators. What was the customs value, and is the figure right?

Step 1, write the relationship. Let V be the customs value. Duty is 0.05V. Import VAT is 10 percent of V plus duty, which is 0.10 times 1.05V, or 0.105V. Total paid at the border is 0.05V plus 0.105V, which is 0.155V.

Step 2, solve. 0.155V equals 57,750 dollars, so V equals 57,750 divided by 0.155, which is 372,581 dollars, roughly.

Step 3, compare with the paperwork. The supplier's invoice says 340,000 dollars. Freight to the port was 30,000 dollars and insurance 2,500 dollars. Cost, insurance and freight is 372,500 dollars. The reconstructed value of about 372,581 dollars matches to within rounding. The broker valued on cost, insurance and freight, which in this hypothetical country is correct.

Step 4, split the payment. Duty: 0.05 times 372,500 equals 18,625 dollars, a cost. Import VAT: 0.105 times 372,500 equals 39,113 dollars, roughly, which is recoverable only if the generators serve taxable supplies. Check: 18,625 plus 39,113 equals 57,738 dollars, within rounding of 57,750.

What if the reconstruction had come out at 420,000 dollars? Then something was added that you did not expect: a royalty, an assist, a different freight basis, or a classification at a higher duty rate. That is the question to send your broker, in writing.

Say that out loud now.

Calculation two: from the overrun back to the decisions

The outcome: a mixed-use project finished 1,000,000 dollars over budget, and the cost consultant says about 900,000 dollars of it is indirect tax. The budget was built net of all VAT. Take the 900,000 dollars apart.

Step 1, separate recoverable from unrecoverable. The VAT ledger shows 3,000,000 dollars of input VAT paid on 30,000,000 dollars of construction, with 600,000 dollars recovered. So 2,400,000 dollars was never recovered. But the budget team says they had already allowed 1,800,000 dollars for unrecoverable VAT in a late revision. Unbudgeted unrecoverable VAT: 2,400,000 minus 1,800,000, which is 600,000 dollars.

Step 2, find why it was 2,400,000 and not 1,800,000. The revision assumed shared-cost VAT would be apportioned by expected rent, with the shops at 35 percent, recovering 700,000 dollars of the 2,000,000 dollars of shared-cost VAT. The authority accepted only floor area, 20 percent, recovering 400,000 dollars. Difference: 300,000 dollars. The remaining 300,000 dollars traces to direct costs coded to the shops that the authority reclassified as shared, because the shops and apartments share the services that serve them. Decision behind it: an apportionment method assumed, not agreed.

Step 3, the reverse charge. Foreign design fees of 1,500,000 dollars were paid with no VAT accounted for. At an audit, reverse-charge VAT of 150,000 dollars was assessed. Of it, 80 percent relates to the exempt residential use on the floor-area method, so 120,000 dollars is unrecoverable, plus interest, say 30,000 dollars. Total: 150,000 dollars. Decision behind it: no reverse-charge check in invoice approval.

Step 4, the customs reclassification. Imported cladding was entered under a heading at 5 percent duty; the authority reclassified it under a heading at 10 percent. On a customs value of 2,000,000 dollars, extra duty is 5 percent, 100,000 dollars. Extra import VAT on the extra duty, 10,000 dollars, is largely unrecoverable on the residential share. Call it 100,000 dollars net. Decision behind it: no written classification from the broker for a high-value item.

Step 5, the refund delay. Refunds of recoverable VAT arrived eight months late. Carrying an average of 300,000 dollars for eight months at a hypothetical 8 percent costs 300,000 times 0.08 times 8 divided by 12, which is 16,000 dollars. Call it 50,000 dollars including the extra interest reserve drawn on the construction loan during the delay. Decision behind it: no VAT facility and no refund timing in the cash flow.

Step 6, reconcile. 600,000 plus 150,000 plus 100,000 plus 50,000 equals 900,000 dollars. Every dollar traced to a decision.

Calculation three: the most you can pay the supplier

Now run the method forward from a target. The cost plan allows 420,000 dollars for a pump package landed on site, and the import VAT will be recoverable because the pumps serve the taxable commercial floors. What is the highest price you can accept from the supplier?

Step 1, the cost that stays in the budget is customs value plus duty, because recoverable import VAT is funded but not a cost. So 1.05V must not exceed 420,000 dollars, and V is at most 400,000 dollars. Step 2, subtract freight of 25,000 dollars and insurance of 3,000 dollars, both quoted. The highest supplier price is 400,000 minus 28,000, which is 372,000 dollars. Step 3, fund the import VAT of 0.10 times 420,000, which is 42,000 dollars, until it is recovered. If instead the pumps served the exempt apartments, the import VAT would be a cost too, the landed cost would be 1.155V, and V could be no more than about 363,600 dollars, cutting the highest supplier price to about 335,600 dollars. The same pump, two different ceilings, decided by what the building does.

What the reverse calculation teaches

Four decisions caused 900,000 dollars of overrun. Assuming an apportionment method instead of agreeing it. Not checking foreign invoices for the reverse charge. Not obtaining a written classification for a large import. Not modelling refund timing. Each costs little to fix at feasibility, and each became expensive because it was discovered at completion.

Professional sign-off required: indirect tax adviser on apportionment and reverse charge; licensed customs broker on valuation and classification; cost consultant on the final reconciliation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting an overrun labelled "tax" as one unexplained number. The control is to reconcile it, line by line, back to the decisions that caused it, and to change the process before the next project.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner checks only that the broker's total looks plausible. Rebuild the customs value from the invoice, freight and insurance, every time the shipment is large.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal: work backward from public information to the implied land price, rent and return. The same habit works on cost. A final number is evidence, and working back from it shows you the assumptions that produced it.

Recap

A border payment of 57,750 dollars rebuilt to a customs value of about 372,500 dollars on cost, insurance and freight. A 900,000 dollar indirect tax overrun traced to an assumed apportionment method, a missed reverse charge, a customs reclassification and unmodelled refund delay.

Next: Devika on The Room: the compliance review with the concession authority.
checklist: I can rebuild any customs payment from value, duty and import VAT.
I compare the rebuilt customs value with the invoice, freight and insurance.
I ask my broker in writing about any unexplained difference.
I reconcile any indirect tax overrun line by line.
I agree the apportionment method with my adviser before relying on it.
Invoice approval includes a reverse-charge check on foreign services.
High-value imports have a written classification before they ship.
Refund timing is modelled in the project cash flow.
head: Field checklist
speak: I reverse engineer indirect tax from the finished number. A broker reports 57,750 dollars paid at the border. With hypothetical duty of five percent and import VAT of ten percent on value plus duty, the total is 15.5 percent of customs value, so the value is about 372,500 dollars, which matches the invoice plus freight and insurance. If it had come out higher, I would ask what was added, or how it was classified. Then an overrun. A project finished 900,000 dollars over budget on indirect tax. Taking it apart: 600,000 from an apportionment method that was assumed rather than agreed, 150,000 from foreign design fees with no reverse charge, 100,000 from a customs reclassification of cladding, and 50,000 from late refunds that were never modelled. Every dollar traced to a decision, and each decision was cheap to get right at feasibility.
terms: Landed cost — the total cost of imported goods once they arrive, including price, freight, insurance, duty and any unrecoverable import taxes.
Cost, insurance and freight (CIF) — a valuation basis that includes the goods' price plus insurance and freight to the port of import.
Binding ruling — a written decision from an authority, where available, on how a specific item will be classified or treated, given before the transaction.

hostile.q: Your final cost report shows 900,000 dollars of tax overrun. How do I know it will not happen on your next project?
hostile.a: Because we traced every dollar to a decision and changed each process. The apportionment method is now agreed with our adviser at feasibility, invoice approval includes a reverse-charge check, every import above a set value gets a written classification before it ships, and refund timing is in the cash flow with a VAT facility behind it. Here is the reconciliation and the revised checklist.

title: The Concession Compliance Review
summary: A scene in which officials from the agency that granted your investment concession, with a customs officer, review whether you have met its conditions. This lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state.
body:
A concession review is not an interrogation; it is the government checking that it received what it paid for, and you pass it by showing, item by item and date by date, that the bargain was kept.

Recall

Q. How do you rebuild a customs value from the total paid at the border?

A. Write duty and import VAT as fractions of the value, add them to get the total as one fraction of value, divide the payment by that fraction, and compare the result with invoice, freight and insurance.

Q. In a transfer pricing audit meeting, what should you ask when an auditor states a provisional view you disagree with?

A. Which part of the analysis leads them there, so the conclusion becomes a point you can address in writing.

Q. What is substantial completion?

A. The stage at which the work is complete enough for the owner to occupy or use it for its intended purpose, with only minor items outstanding. Its contractual definition decides what follows, such as release of retainage.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if your project depends on a concession, this meeting can decide hundreds of thousands of dollars and your standing with an agency you will need again. In many emerging markets, the investment agency is also your route to approvals, work permits and future concessions. How you handle a review is remembered.

The scene

This is a hypothetical scene. Eighteen months into construction of a hotel built under a concession that relieves customs duty and import VAT on listed items. Two officials from the investment agency and one customs officer visit the site office. With you are your concession owner, the person Rule 62 requires, and your customs broker. On the table: the concession register, the condition calendar and the quarterly self-audits.

The lead official opens: "We want to confirm that the relieved goods are in this project, that the investment commitments are on track, and that the opening date will be met."

The customs officer adds: "Our records show 214 entries under your concession. Can you show us where each item is?"

The lines to say

"Thank you. Each of the 214 entries is in our register, with its customs entry number, description, value, relief claimed and installed location by drawing reference. Our concession owner will walk you through it, and we can visit any location you choose."

On the investment commitment: "Our committed investment to date is shown on page 3, reconciled to the audited accounts. Employment figures are on page 4, from payroll."

On the opening date: "Our current programme shows opening four months later than the concession date, because of a financing delay. We submitted an extension request two months ago, which is in the file with your acknowledgement. If the agency needs anything further to decide it, please tell us today."

On a known problem: "Our quarterly self-audit found one pallet of tiles moved to a staff accommodation block that is not part of the approved project. We have quantified the duty and VAT on that pallet, here is the calculation, and we are ready to pay it or return the tiles to the hotel, whichever the agency prefers."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say "we'll have to check where those went" about a relieved item. If the register cannot answer, write down the entry number and commit to a written answer by a date, but understand that this is the weakest moment in the meeting.

Never say "the contractor handled the imports" as a defence. The concession is yours, and the officials will hold you to it.

Never say "surely a few months' delay doesn't matter." Whether it matters is their decision under the instrument, and minimising it signals that you have not read the conditions.

Never offer a gift, a meal, a favour, a donation or any other thing of value to the officials, and never discuss "speeding things up". In many countries even the appearance of it is an offence, and anti-bribery laws can reach you from abroad. Verify the laws that apply against the primary source, and report any request to your lawyer.

The question behind the question

Behind "show us where each item is" is: did relieved goods leak into the local market or other projects, where they would compete with goods on which duty was paid? That is the abuse concession regimes most fear. Behind the investment and jobs questions is: did the country get the investment it gave up revenue for? And behind the date is: is this project still real, or is the concession being used to import goods for something else?

Answer those three underlying questions and the specific ones become easy.

When to stay silent

When an official is reading the register or walking the site, let them. Do not narrate. When you disclose the moved pallet, state it, give the calculation, and then stop; do not soften it with explanations about how busy the site was. When an official says "we will consider the extension", do not press for a decision in the room. Ask only: "Is there anything further you need from us, and by when?"

How to hold your state

Officials notice whether you are composed. Arrive early, read the register the night before, and know the three hardest facts: the delay, the pallet, and any entry the self-audit could not close. Speak slowly, use the agency's own terms from the concession instrument, and let your concession owner and broker answer the detail. If you feel defensive, point to a page. Breathing drills belong before you walk in, parked and seated, never while driving to the site; check with your doctor if you have any condition that might be affected.

After the review

Within two working days, write to the agency: what was reviewed, what was provided, the disclosed pallet and the proposed settlement, the status of the extension request, and any item to follow, with dates. Copy your lawyer. Then update the register and the calendar with the review itself, because the next review will ask what the last one found.

How the best do it

Developers who rely on concessions repeatedly treat the agency as a long-term counterparty. They appoint one person as the single point of contact, report proactively before the agency asks, disclose problems themselves, and keep every commitment on its date. Over time that record is worth more than any single concession, because agencies extend discretion to investors who have shown they do not need watching. A small developer can copy this with a quarterly one-page compliance letter to the agency, sent whether or not anyone asked for it.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer on the concession instrument, the extension request and any settlement; licensed customs broker on the register.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is walking into the review without having audited yourself first, so the agency finds the problems. The control is the quarterly self-audit Rule 62 requires, and disclosure of what it finds before anyone asks.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the review as a hostile inspection and stays guarded. The agency is checking a bargain; transparency is the stronger position.

Callback

In Week 32, Pax and REGA taught that entitlements come with conditions, and that a development agreement binds the developer long after the approval. A concession is the tax and customs version of the same bargain, and the conditions survive completion of the building.

Recap

Show the officials, item by item, that relieved goods are in the project, that investment and jobs are on track, and that the date is met or an extension was requested in time. Disclose problems yourself, quantify them, stay silent while they read, offer nothing of value, and confirm in writing.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: indirect taxes, with a Red Pen drill on a pro forma's VAT and duty lines.
checklist: I have read the concession register and calendar the night before the review.
I know the three hardest facts and have answers with documents.
Every relieved entry can be located by drawing reference.
Any extension request was made before the deadline and is in the file.
I disclose self-audit findings with a calculation and a proposed settlement.
I never blame the contractor for a concession I hold.
I offer nothing of value to any official and report any request to my lawyer.
I confirm the review's outcome in writing within two working days.
head: Field checklist
speak: A concession review is the government checking that it received what it gave up revenue for. Behind every question are three: did relieved goods leak into the local market or other projects, did the country get the investment and jobs it was promised, and is the project still real and on time. So I bring the register, with every customs entry tied to an installed location, the investment and payroll figures reconciled to the accounts, and the extension request I filed before the date passed. If my own audit found a problem, a pallet of tiles moved to the wrong building, I disclose it with the calculation and offer to pay or return the goods. I never blame the contractor, never minimise a delay, and never offer anything of value to an official. I let them read in silence, and I confirm everything in writing within two days.
terms: Compliance review — an inspection by the granting agency or customs to confirm that a concession's conditions have been met.
Single point of contact — one named person who handles all communication with an agency, keeping commitments consistent.
Extension request — a written application, made before a deadline, asking the agency to extend a concession condition, with reasons.

hostile.q: Your hotel will open four months after the concession date. Why shouldn't we withdraw the relief on everything you have imported?
hostile.a: Because the goods are in the approved project, which we can show you entry by entry, and because we applied for an extension two months before the date, with the reasons and a revised programme, and you acknowledged it. The investment and employment commitments are on track, as pages 3 and 4 show. The one item our audit found outside the project, a pallet of tiles, we have disclosed and quantified, and we will pay the duty on it or return it to the hotel today.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 62 Review: Indirect Taxes, Customs and Concessions
summary: Six questions on VAT and GST, exempt supplies, apportionment, the reverse charge, customs duty and Rule 62, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a pro forma's indirect tax lines, and a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: indirect tax is charged on transactions from the first invoice, so classify every supply, budget gross, account for imports and foreign services correctly, and treat every concession as a contract with conditions.

Recall

Q. In a concession review, what are the three questions behind the officials' questions?

A. Did relieved goods leak outside the project, did the country get the promised investment and jobs, and is the project still real and on time?

Q. In transfer pricing, what is a benchmarking study?

A. A documented search for comparable transactions or companies used to set an arm's-length range for a related-party price.

Q. What is a non-conformance report?

A. A formal record that work or material does not meet the specification, starting a process of review, decision and corrective action.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, indirect tax is the cost that hides in other people's invoices. If you can answer these six questions aloud, you can read a budget, a customs entry and a concession instrument and see where money will leak. Answer each before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. How does VAT or GST reach the final consumer without being charged twice along the chain?

Answer: Each registered business charges output tax on its sales and deducts the input tax it paid on purchases, paying only the difference. The final consumer, who cannot deduct anything, bears the whole tax.

Question 2. What is the difference between a zero-rated supply and an exempt supply, and why does it matter to a landlord?

Answer: Both carry no tax on the sale, but a zero-rated supplier still recovers input tax and an exempt supplier does not. A landlord letting exempt residential space therefore cannot recover the construction VAT, which becomes part of the building's cost.

Question 3. How is input VAT on shared costs treated in a mixed-use building?

Answer: It is apportioned between taxable and exempt uses by a method accepted under local law, such as floor area, and only the taxable share is recoverable. Some systems adjust the split later if actual use changes.

Question 4. What does a reverse charge require, and when is it a real cost?

Answer: The buyer of certain services from abroad accounts for the VAT itself. It nets to zero if the buyer's supplies are fully taxable, but it is a real cost when they are exempt.

Question 5. What three things decide customs duty on an import?

Answer: Value, often the price plus freight and insurance to the border; classification under the Harmonized System, which sets the rate; and origin, which decides whether a preferential rate applies.

Question 6. What is Rule 62?

Answer: Never use a tax or duty concession without a register that ties every relieved item to its approved use, and a dated calendar of every condition, owned by a named person and reviewed every month.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Devika set out how VAT and GST work, the three categories of supply, customs duty and the investment concession. Ford and Cole took apart a composite in which a concession was clawed back after goods moved, a date passed and records were missing, giving Rule 62. Priya priced apportionment, the funding of recoverable VAT and the change from sale to rent. Devika taught registration, time and place of supply, the reverse charge, customs valuation and classification, and the seven questions for a concession. She reverse engineered a border payment and a 900,000 dollar overrun. Then she ran the concession compliance review.

Red Pen

Read these hypothetical pro forma lines and notes for a mixed-use building with shops and rented apartments, and find the defects before reading on.

Hard cost: 30,000,000 dollars, net of VAT (all VAT recoverable). Imported cladding and lifts: 3,000,000 dollars, ex-works supplier price, duty nil under concession. Design fees, foreign architect: 1,200,000 dollars, no VAT charged. VAT refunds: assumed received in the month paid. Concession: relief on all imports for the project; conditions per agreement. Contingency: 5 percent of hard cost. Plan: sell apartments if the market is strong at completion, otherwise rent.

The defects. First, "all VAT recoverable" is wrong for a building that rents apartments, where residential rent is often exempt; the residential and apportioned shared-cost VAT is cost and is missing. Second, an ex-works price is not the customs value in a country that values on cost, insurance and freight, and freight, insurance and any unrecoverable import VAT are missing from the landed cost. Third, "duty nil under concession" assumes the lifts and cladding are on the concession's list and imported in the right name; the note does not say. Fourth, a foreign architect charging no VAT does not mean none is due; a reverse charge may apply, and on the exempt share it is a real cost. Fifth, refunds received in the month paid ignores refund lag and unfunded VAT during construction. Sixth, "relief on all imports" overstates what concessions usually cover, and "conditions per agreement" means nobody has listed them, which Rule 62 forbids. Seventh, contingency of 5 percent of a net figure is too thin when indirect tax is unpriced, and contingency is not a place to hide a known cost. Eighth, "sell or rent at completion" is an indirect tax decision deferred: changing from sale to rent can claw back credits claimed on the assumption of sale.

The corrected version builds cost gross, shows recoverable and unrecoverable VAT separately with an agreed apportionment, values imports on the correct basis with duty confirmed against the concession list, accounts for the reverse charge, models refund timing and a VAT facility, lists every concession condition in a calendar, and prices both the sale and the rent cases.

Kema's method for any Red Pen applies again: read once for what is being bought or sold, once for how each number is built and whether its source is outside your own assumptions, and once for what has been deferred to later. Most indirect tax defects hide in the third reading, in a decision written as if it could be made at completion without cost.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a lender's credit committee that asks, "How have you dealt with VAT and duty on this project?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Our budget is built gross of VAT. The shops are taxable, so their VAT is recoverable. The apartments will be rented, which our adviser classifies as exempt, so the VAT on them, and their share of shared costs on a floor-area split our adviser confirmed is accepted, is in the budget as a cost. Recoverable VAT is funded by a facility repaid from refunds, with refund lag modelled. Foreign design fees are subject to a reverse charge, which we account for. Imports are valued on the correct basis, and the main packages have written classifications from our broker. Our concession covers listed items only; every relieved import is in a register tied to its installed location, every condition is in a calendar with a named owner, and we self-audit quarterly. If we ever change from rent to sale or back, we have priced the adjustment."

Score yourself. Did you open with gross budgeting? Did you name exempt residential rent? The reverse charge? The concession register? Under two minutes?

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a budget built net of VAT on a building that makes exempt supplies, combined with a concession nobody is managing. The control is a gross budget, an indirect tax memo at feasibility and Rule 62.

The beginner's mistake

Treating indirect tax as the accountant's problem at year end. It is a design, procurement and budgeting decision from the first pro forma.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage built sources and uses and taught that contingency is a priced estimate of what you do not know. Unrecoverable VAT is not unknown; it is a known cost that belongs on its own line in the uses, and hiding it in contingency spends the contingency before construction starts.

Recap

Classify every supply, budget gross, apportion by an accepted method, fund refunds, account for the reverse charge, value and classify imports correctly, and manage every concession with a register and calendar.

checklist: How does VAT or GST reach the final consumer without being charged twice along the chain?
What is the difference between a zero-rated supply and an exempt supply, and why does it matter to a landlord?
How is input VAT on shared costs treated in a mixed-use building?
What does a reverse charge require, and when is it a real cost?
What three things decide customs duty on an import?
What is Rule 62?
head: The six questions
speak: Indirect tax is charged on transactions from the first invoice, not on profit. VAT or GST is charged by registered businesses, each deducting the tax it paid on purchases, so the final consumer bears it. Zero-rated sales keep that deduction; exempt sales lose it, which is why a landlord renting exempt residential space pays construction VAT as a cost. In a mixed-use building, VAT on shared costs is split by an accepted method, and recoverable VAT still has to be funded until refunds arrive. Services bought from abroad can carry a reverse charge, a real cost on exempt supplies. Customs duty depends on value, classification and origin, and is usually a pure cost. A concession relieves these taxes only on listed items and only while its conditions are met, so I keep a register, a dated calendar of conditions and a named owner, and I budget gross from day one.
terms: Output tax — the VAT or GST a registered business charges on its sales.
Zero-rated supply — a sale taxed at zero percent, on which the seller can still recover input tax.
Landed cost — the total cost of imported goods on arrival, including price, freight, insurance, duty and unrecoverable import taxes.

hostile.q: Your pro forma shows hard cost net of VAT and nil duty on imports. Prove those two assumptions.
hostile.a: Neither assumption survives in our revised budget. Hard cost is now gross of VAT, with the recoverable commercial share and the unrecoverable residential share shown separately on an apportionment our adviser confirmed. Duty is nil only on the items listed in the concession and imported in the project company's name; here is the list, the register and the broker's classifications. Anything outside the list carries duty in the budget.
